title: The First Road Trip
summary: Josh and Chuck tell the story of the first cross-country automobile trip: Horatio Nelson Jackson and mechanic Sewell Crocker's 1903 drive from San Francisco to New York in a Winton touring car, with the dog Bud. They cover the poor state of American roads in 1900, earlier failed attempts (the Davis couple in 1899, Alexander Winton in 1901), the $1,500 wager at the University Club, the rival Packard and Oldsmobile sponsored trips, the route north through Oregon, breakdowns, the trip's arrival in Manhattan on July 26, 1903, and later events including Alice Ramsey's 1909 trip and Cannonball Baker's record. The episode also includes a segue-off-a-cliff tangent and a listener mail factoid about the Amazon's outflow.

segments.title: Opening and context
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the story of Horatio Nelson Jackson's first cross-country car trip, credit Ken Burns' documentary Horatio's Drive and Dayton Duncan's book, and describe the early 1900s context of rail travel, poor roads, few cars, and lack of maps.

segments.title: Early failed cross-country attempts
segments.summary: Car companies sponsored publicity drives. The Davis couple, sponsored by National Motor Carriage Company in 1899, lost a race to a one-armed bicyclist and dropped out after Chicago. Alexander Winton then tried in about 1901 and got stuck in a Nevada sand dune.

segments.title: The wager and choosing the car
segments.summary: Jackson bets about $1,500 at the University Club of San Francisco that he can drive to New York in under 90 days. Jackson, a former doctor with a wealthy wife Bertha, picks Sewell Crocker as mechanic and buys a used 1903 Winton touring car, which they name the Vermont.

segments.title: The open car and rival corporate teams
segments.summary: The hosts describe the open, unprotected Winton with about 20 horsepower and a 30 mph top speed. They contrast Jackson's self-funded trip with the sponsored Packard and Oldsmobile teams that had mechanics and pre-positioned gasoline.

segments.title: Gear, route choice, and the railroad rights-of-way
segments.summary: They pack camping gear, rope, a block and tackle, and guns, and lose items along the way. They choose to go west to east and route north through Oregon to avoid the Nevada desert, using railroad rights-of-way and bridges.

segments.title: Departure, breakdowns, and mountain roads
segments.summary: They leave San Francisco on May 23, 1903, and blow tires early. Tires, tubes, and clutch failures are recurring problems, along with getting stuck and misdirected by locals. Crocker repeatedly repairs the clutch and they use the block and tackle to escape mud. The hosts explain what a clutch does.

segments.title: Segue cliff legend tangent
segments.summary: After the break the hosts check a claim that a Segway rider drove off a cliff. BBC reports Jimmy Hezeldin, 62, died riding his company's Segways in West Yorkshire. They also briefly discuss a Fabio roller coaster meme they could not verify.

segments.title: Bud the dog and the trip's later stretch
segments.summary: In Caldwell, Idaho, Jackson and Crocker acquire a pit bull named Bud, who rides as mascot and is fitted with goggles; they paid $15 for him. Press coverage grows. After Wyoming and Omaha the roads improve, and they make about 70 miles in a day.

segments.title: Cleveland, Buffalo wreck, and arrival in New York
segments.summary: In Cleveland Winton offers sponsorship, which Jackson declines. In Buffalo the car crashes into a hidden obstruction and the three are ejected, but nobody is hurt. They reach Manhattan on July 26, 1903, after 63 days, 12 hours and 30 minutes. Jackson never collects the wager.

segments.title: Aftermath and later records
segments.summary: Bud lived out his days on the Jackson farm in Vermont. Jackson later ran businesses, served in World War One, and ran for governor of Vermont. He donated the Vermont car to the Smithsonian. Crocker died young around 1913 after a Mexico assignment. Alice Ramsey made the first all-woman trip in 59 days in 1909, and Cannonball Baker's 1930s record led to the Cannonball Run.

segments.title: Listener mail: Amazon factoid
segments.summary: Rich Pope writes in with a factoid: the volume of water leaving the Amazon's mouth equals that of Niagara, Victoria, and Iguazu Falls combined, multiplied by twelve.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and close the episode with the show's production credit.
